documents.abstract: Awe has attracted substantial scholarly attention, but its implications for management remains fragmented across different accounts of what awe is and why it matters. In this review, we first show that the literature has developed around three dominant perspectives—collective self, epistemic, and well-being—each of which offers a distinct account of awe’s primary function. To integrate these perspectives, we advance a metamorphosis model of awe, which explains how awe first breaks down self- and nonself-schemata before building them back up again, producing an expansion of mind and self. We then organize the diverse elicitors of awe into cognitive, physical, social, and technological sources, clarifying the conditions under which awe is likely to arise. Through this model, we portray awe as a transformative emotion that influences identity, cognition, and behavior, with implications for core organizational processes such as leadership, work design, organizational change, sensemaking, and innovation. We conclude by charting a forward-looking research agenda calling for greater examination of awe’s role at the individual, team, and organizational levels.

Bash scripts underpin system administration, DevOps automation, and Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD), where code quality directly determines system stability and security. Yet when Large Language Models (LLMs) are tasked with generating such scripts, two problems compound each other: models produce code without any accompanying justification for their design choices, and this absence of scrutiny correlates with scripts that silently harbor robustness flaws, including mishandled edge cases, unchecked failure modes, and fragile assumptions about the execution environment. We present BashCoder-R1, a framework that tackles both problems jointly, treating explainability as a design goal rather than a byproduct of correctness. The training pipeline proceeds in three stages. Continual Pre-training (CPT) first adapts the base model to the syntactic conventions and idioms specific to Bash. We then curate thousands of expert-validated reasoning-and-code samples and use them for Long Chain-of-Thought Supervised Fine-Tuning (L-CoT SFT), training the model to reproduce the deliberative, risk-averse thinking pattern of an experienced system administrator before it writes any code. Finally, Robustness-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (R-GRPO) directly refines the generation policy against a weighted reward combining syntax correctness, robustness as verified by the static analyzer shellcheck , and adherence to the required reasoning format. We evaluate BashCoder-R1 on BashBench , a benchmark we construct from 952 real-world automation tasks (773 single-line commands and 179 multi-line scripts), against a wide range of state-of-the-art baselines. BashCoder-R1 attains SyntaxPass of 100.00% / 94.97%, RobustWarnRate of 4.01% / 16.47%, RobustPass of 95.99% / 79.33%, FuncRate of 93.01% / 93.85%, and FullRate of 90.04% / 73.18% on single-line / multi-line tasks respectively, a relative FullRate improvement of 37.82% and 20.18% over the strongest baseline, DeepSeek-V3.2 (Reasoning). Human evaluation across Functionality, Robustness, and Clarity further confirms that BashCoder-R1's reasoning chains are rated highest in quality among all compared systems.

Helicobacterpylori (H. pylori) infection is a significant health issue. It is classified by the World Health Organization as a Group I carcinogen. Egypt has unusually high prevalence rates of 64.6–90.3%, significantly above the global averages. Histopathological diagnosis is tedious and time-consuming and has high interobserver variation, especially with small, scattered bacterial colonies. This study represents the first comprehensive application of artificial intelligence to this diagnostic task. We compared eight state-of-the-art architectures. The models were trained for 50 epochs and assessed on 100 histopathological whole-slide images using metrics including accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and AUC-ROC. MobileNetV2 and Xception performed perfectly with 100% accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, an AUC of 1.0, and zero misclassifications. MobileNetV2 was trained 2.3 times faster, offering an efficiency advantage relevant to deployment in resource-limited pathology laboratories, pending external validation. Another four models (DenseNet-201, InceptionV3, VGG-16, and VGG-19) recorded 100% test accuracy, while Vision Transformer recorded 96.97%. These results represent retrospective patch-level classification performance and do not constitute clinical diagnostic validation. This study not only establishes the first validated artificial intelligence classification system of H. pylori in Egypt but also shows high performance on Egyptian samples and offers a solid methodological groundwork for future medical AI applications in resource-constrained contexts.

Be is a proposed organization dedicated to making safe, professionally governed artificial intelligence emotional support freely accessible to people who need someone to talk to. Be proposes an AI emotional-support system designed around a foundational distinction: an AI must never confuse what it observes with what it infers. Version 2.0 further develops the proposal's framework for adaptive conversational communication through the principle Adaptive Tone, Fixed Boundaries. Be may adapt its tone, vocabulary, pacing, humor, warmth, and conversational style to meet an individual where they are, while maintaining fixed ethical and relational boundaries. The system should allow human-like communication without creating a false human identity, adapting the interface without fabricating the relationship. The proposal incorporates Red Tape Theory™ as a proposed safety methodology: Observe. Record. Question. Do not force the axiom. Interpretation must never be represented as observation. Be does not propose to diagnose users or replace licensed mental-health professionals. Instead, it proposes a professionally governed pathway through which an AI system may recognize when AI-only support may no longer be an appropriate level of support and facilitate access to human care. A proposed charitable human-care program, If You Get It, You Get It, would seek to use charitable resources to help people access licensed professional care when professionally established safety criteria indicate that additional human support may be appropriate. Version 2.0 expands the proposal's treatment of personalization as a safety boundary, including the distinction between adapting communication to an individual and constructing a misleading simulated relationship. It also addresses clinical governance, privacy, autonomy, human handoff, crisis safety, documentation, intellectual-property considerations, research and evaluation, and a potential future child-focused system provisionally called NewBee. This publication is a founding proposal and does not represent a deployed clinical service, licensed mental-health treatment program, clinical efficacy claim, professional endorsement, or completed charitable program. Be begins with the question: Where could this harm somebody?

Be proposes an AI emotional-support system designed around a foundational distinction: an AI must never confuse what it observes with what it infers. The proposed system combines adaptive conversational communication with fixed ethical and relational boundaries. Be may adapt its tone, vocabulary, pacing, humor, warmth, and conversational style to meet an individual where they are, while maintaining transparency about its identity as an AI and avoiding manufactured intimacy, emotional dependency, or deceptive human-like identity. The project incorporates Red Tape Theory™ as a proposed safety methodology: Observe. Record. Question. Do not force the axiom. Be does not propose to diagnose users or replace licensed mental-health professionals. Instead, it proposes a professionally governed pathway through which an AI system may recognize when AI-only support may no longer be an appropriate level of support and facilitate access to human care. A proposed charitable human-care program, If You Get It, You Get It, would seek to use charitable resources to help people access licensed professional care when professionally established safety criteria indicate that additional human support may be appropriate. The proposal also addresses clinical governance, privacy, autonomy, human handoff, crisis safety, documentation, intellectual-property considerations, research and evaluation, adaptive personalization, and a potential future child-focused system provisionally called NewBee. This publication is a founding proposal and does not represent a deployed clinical service, licensed mental-health treatment program, clinical efficacy claim, professional endorsement, or completed charitable program. Be begins with the question: Where could this harm somebody?

documents.abstract: Within the shared industry vision of AI-RAN, AI-and-RAN seeks to co-locate virtualized radio access network (vRAN) workloads and AI services on shared GPUs. This sharing is inherently asymmetric: vRAN workload is latency-critical, whereas the machine learning (ML) workload is a throughput-oriented, best-effort co-tenant. We present Beaver, a GPU sharing system that jointly manages compute and memory resources while protecting the vRAN's strict processing deadline. Beaver sizes the vRAN's streaming multiprocessor (SM) allocation from each slot's scheduled workload, repartitions SM allocations at slot granularity, and rewrites compiled ML kernels to yield HBM bandwidth during the vRAN's memory-critical phases. We implement Beaver and evaluate it using NVIDIA Aerial with heterogeneous multi-cell workloads, real-world cellular traces, production inference kernels, and full-stack LLM serving. On an H200 GPU, Beaver keeps the vRAN's p99.9 latency within its 1.5ms uplink deadline while retaining 74% of Llama-3.3-70B serving throughput. It also incurs no observed deadline misses under replayed cellular traces, protects a 375us downlink deadline, and generalizes to other GPUs including A100, GB10 and GH200.

Purpose This study investigates the entanglement of researcher’s agency and authorship in curriculum development mediated by generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Despite growing enthusiasm for GenAI’s transformative potential, little is known about the process of becoming-with AI in the epistemic and ethical labor of design. Guided by the research question – what forms of agency and authorship emerge through the process of becoming-with AI in AI-mediated curriculum design? Design/methodology/approach Employing a hermeneutic autoethnographic methodology, the researcher documented a lived experience through iterative interactions with GenAI across curriculum planning, sequencing, mapping, alignment and implementation. Data sources included structured prompting protocols, reflective analytic memos and Photovoice artifacts capturing critical decision points in AI-assisted design. Findings Qualitative content analysis has revealed five configurations in curriculum work: GenAI as a mediator of curricular coherence, an architect of sequencing learning, a cartographer of curricular alignment, a curator of contextualized learning experiences and an orchestrator of aligned and active learning. Originality/value Findings indicate that agency and authorship are not diminished in AI-mediated contexts but reconstituted as distributed and ethically intensified practices. GenAI redistributes cognitive labor while amplifying the need for disciplined discernment in evaluating alignment, coherence and epistemic integrity. Curriculum development thus emerges as a negotiated sociotechnical practice in which professional judgment remains the locus of accountability.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful paradigm for training agents, yet its success rests on domain expertise of human engineers who design informative reward signals for every new task. Unsupervised RL aims to reduce this engineering with intrinsic motivation (IM): reward signals that emerge from the agent environment interaction itself. Existing IM objectives, however, involve the selection of information variables, which re-introduces domain expertise the field has sought to eliminate. We introduce Forward CIP (F-CIP), an RL-native formulation of the Controllable Information Production (CIP) objective, which is defined by the system's dynamics alone and requires no such selection. We prove that F-CIP is compatible with RL and demonstrate its effectiveness with existing algorithms. Training agents with F-CIP results in unsupervised discovery of primitive behaviors such as balancing and maintaining controllability, which are essential for more complex robot behaviors. Paired with a simple forward-velocity reward, our method produces coordinated gaits such as hopping and running which otherwise require reward engineering to learn.

Quantum AI is a new way to think about the future of Artificial Intelligence through the merging of two technologies: quantum computing and advanced machine learning. Quantum AI has the potential to provide solutions to computationally difficult problems that traditional systems cannot solve. Quantum AI's continued success will rely on advancements in hybrid quantum-classical solutions, as well as the expansion of quantum hardware; hence, research remains necessary to conduct systematic benchmarks as well as performance analysis in order to determine both how well quantum AI algorithms perform practically, and where their limitations lie. In this chapter, detailed examinations of benchmarks that have been developed specifically for quantum AI are presented alongside evaluative metrics across various key areas of performance including algorithmic efficiency, scalability, noise immunity, and resource use for various types of quantum architectures. The chapter integrates dialogue between theory and practice to demonstrate ways in which performance metrics (i.e., quantum circuit depth, fidelity, convergence behaviour and computational complexity) can effectively compare Quantum AI algorithms to classical algorithms. Particular attention is given to hybrid variational algorithms, quantum-enhanced optimization algorithms, and quantum machine learning. Using benchmark datasets, simulation frameworks and new evaluation methods, there are several challenges in terms of reproducibility, hardware variability and algorithm/hardware co-design that emerge through analysis of the above metrics as well. Aside from focusing on a more broad view of how Performance Evaluation relates to developing more effective Quantum AI Solutions. In addition to viewing Benchmarking as a technical exercise solely, this chapter provides a more holistic view in relation to a human perspective of the situation. This paper outlines how performance evaluation practices can be used as a considerable and well-designed means of bridging the gap between the promise of Quantum Technology at an abstract level, and the ability of Quantum Technology to produce tangible outcomes in the real world by adopting a more comprehensive Governance-oriented approach to Benchmarking Quantum AI Systems. The purpose of this chapter is to assist the growing community of researchers, practitioners, and Strategic Technology Professionals by providing them with a clear and structured framework for Evaluation of Quantum AI Algorithms. There is a significant focus of the chapter on establishing important reference points that organizations can use to determine when an intelligent system has successfully achieved a true and validated quantum advantage. The ultimate goal is to assist in guiding the responsible development and implementation of Quantum AI to enable the Potential Benefits of Quantum AI to be realized, in ways that are meaningful and impactful.

Introduction. Generative AI has intensified tensions between news organisations and technology platforms over intellectual property, audience traffic and journalism’s economic sustainability. The report examines how leading Spanish digital media have framed AI since ChatGPT’s emergence, while considering the subsequent disruption caused by Google AI Overviews and AI Mode. Methods. The study combines quantitative content analysis with legal and industry analysis. It examines 242 AI-related articles published between January 2022 and December 2024 by leading Spanish digital-native and legacy outlets, selected according to GfK DAM audience data. Frequency distributions and contingency tables assess thematic frames and editorial positions. Results. Intellectual property emerges as the central underlying conflict. Coverage concentrates on authorship (68%), ethics and legal liability (45%), business models and licensing (32%), and employment (21%). Legacy media generally frame AI as a threat to journalistic assets, whereas digital-native outlets emphasise efficiency and commercial opportunities. Civil society and journalists themselves remain marginal in the debate. Google’s AI-generated summaries further intensify concerns by retaining users within the platform and reducing referral traffic. Discussion. Intellectual property is becoming both a defensive right and a bargaining asset. The sector is consequently shifting from litigation towards licensing, collective negotiation and technological adaptation, although confidential agreements may strengthen major publishers while marginalising smaller outlets.

Human Origin: a process-review label for human-made creative work Concept, method and pilot design Camille G.ORCID: 0009-0009-0364-6396Loch Ness Version 1.0 — 30 September 2026 Pilot website: human-origin-label.lochness-paris.com Abstract Generative AI has made it inexpensive to produce text, images, music and video that appear human-made, and inexpensive to label such work as human-made. Automated AI detectors are not sufficiently reliable to settle questions of authorship, while several existing human-made labels rely primarily on the creator's own declaration. This paper presents Human Origin, a label designed to assess how a work was made rather than what the finished work looks like. A human reviewer examines evidence of the creative process, either during a live video call or through a screen recording containing a one-time code. The reviewer records the outcome on a public, numbered verification page. The proposed system has two visually distinct levels—reviewed and self-declared—as well as revoked status. Badges are served dynamically so that revocation can propagate to displayed badges, and the system monitors the domains on which reviewed badges appear. A discipline-specific Creator Charter defines the permitted and prohibited uses of AI for writing, illustration, photography, music and video. This paper describes the design principles, review procedure, evidence requirements, badge architecture, limitations, threat model and pilot roadmap of Human Origin. Keywords: human-made content; generative AI; authorship; certification label; provenance; process evidence; trust marks; creators 1. Introduction and problem statement Creators who make their work themselves face a new form of uncertainty. A human-written essay, hand-drawn illustration or recorded track can be questioned simply because a machine could have produced something similar. At the same time, generated content can be presented as human-made at very low cost. Automated AI detection does not resolve this problem reliably. An independent test of 14 detection tools found that all scored below 80% accuracy and only five exceeded 70%, with performance declining further when AI-generated text was edited or paraphrased [1]. OpenAI withdrew its own AI text classifier in July 2023, citing its low accuracy [2]. Detector performance can also be uneven across populations: a Stanford study reported that seven detectors incorrectly classified, on average, 61% of essays written by non-native English speakers as AI-generated [3]. A detector score is therefore a weak basis for decisions concerning individual creators. Labels have emerged in response. Several widely used labels are primarily declarative: creators state that their work is human-made without an independent review of the production process. Not By AI, for example, explicitly describes itself as not being an AI-detection tool and relies on creators following its 90% human rule [4]. The Authors Guild's Human Authored certification operates on an honor system supported by a signed license and public database [5][6]. Declarative labels can be useful statements of intent and are comparatively easy to adopt. However, they cannot independently distinguish a genuine declaration from a false one. Human Origin explores a different approach: review the evidence of the creative process rather than attempt to infer authorship from the finished artifact. 2. Related initiatives Several services now provide forms of evidence-based or declarative certification, often using numbered certificates or publicly verifiable records. Their approaches differ principally in who assesses the evidence, what evidence is considered and what information is retained. Initiative Assessment model Notable features Not By AI [4] Self-declared Widely used badges; creators follow a 90% human rule Authors Guild Human Authored [5][6] Honor system; signed license Numbered mark for books; public database Officially Human Art [7] Self-declaration registry with uploaded evidence Certificate ID, QR code, embeddable badges; tier based on amount of evidence Humanmade [8] Hand verification by staff Earlier work, online presence and timelapses; free pledge level and paid certification options HUMA Certificate [9] Expert review and automated forensic tools Four categories of AI involvement; one-year validity The Human Made Mark [10] Review of production materials Film and television; unique number shown in credits Human Origin belongs to the broader evidence-based certification family. Its distinguishing design choices are: review of the creative process itself; no routine retention of creators' source files; dynamically served badges whose revoked status can propagate; monitoring of where reviewed badges are displayed; and discipline-specific standards defining what the certification does and does not cover. 3. Design principles 3.1 Process over product A finished work cannot, by itself, establish how it was produced. The review therefore focuses on traces of the creative process, including: drafts; version histories; layered source files; raw captures; project files; notes and outlines; and other discipline-specific production evidence. The objective is not to identify whether a finished artifact looks human-made, but to examine whether the available process evidence is consistent with the creator's account. 3.2 Claims no stronger than the evidence Human Origin does not claim that no AI tool was ever used. Instead, the label records that an independent reviewer examined the creative process associated with a specified work, using a specified method, on a specified date. The scope of the certification is therefore explicitly limited to the work and process described on the verification page. 3.3 Two levels that cannot be confused Human Origin distinguishes between: Reviewed — the creative process has been examined under the Human Origin review procedure; Self-declared — the creator makes the declaration, but the process has not been independently reviewed; and Revoked — a previously issued reviewed status is no longer valid. The badge system uses visually distinct colours: green for reviewed; orange for self-declared; and red for revoked. Status is also expressed through text and icons so that the distinction does not depend on colour perception. 3.4 Public verifiability Every reviewed badge has a unique number resolving to a public verification page. The verification page records, as applicable: creator; discipline(s); work covered; review date; review method; evidence examined; official website; official social accounts; current status; and an explanation of what the badge does and does not certify. 3.5 Trust that can be lost A badge may be revoked when the applicable standard is breached. Because badges are served dynamically by the Human Origin server, a revoked badge can change to a revoked state wherever it is displayed, subject to caching behaviour. 3.6 Data minimisation Human Origin does not routinely collect or retain creators' source files. During live reviews, the creator shares their screen and files remain on the creator's device. No recording is made by the reviewer. Where a creator submits a screen recording, the recording is transmitted through an accepted encrypted or expiring channel and is deleted within seven days of the decision. 3.7 A standard for each discipline A Creator Charter defines permitted and prohibited uses of AI for each covered discipline. Examples include: Discipline Example of permitted use Example of prohibited use Writing Spelling correction AI-drafted text Illustration Non-generative production tools Generative image creation Photography Noise reduction Generative fill Music Conventional production/editing tools Generative composition Video Conventional editing Generative creation of substantive footage The complete discipline-specific standards are part of the Human Origin pilot documentation. 4. Review methodology 4.1 Application A creator applies by email and provides: a link to the work to be reviewed; and the websites and accounts on which the creator intends to display the badge. This information determines the certification scope, including the work covered, recorded on the public verification page. 4.2 Review modes Two review modes are proposed. 4.2.1 Live review The creator participates in a video call of approximately 30 minutes. During the call, the creator shares their screen and opens relevant files and production evidence. Nothing is sent to the reviewer and the session is not recorded by the reviewer. 4.2.2 Screen-recording review The creator makes a screen recording showing the relevant files and production evidence. Immediately before recording, the reviewer sends a one-time code. The creator displays or enters the code during the recording, providing evidence that the recording was produced specifically for the review. Accepted transmission channels include: Signal disappearing messages; WhatsApp disappearing messages; Threema disappearing messages; Telegram Secret Chats; expiring Proton Drive links; and expiring SwissTransfer links. The review method used is recorded on the public verification page. 4.3 Evidence by discipline Discipline Typical evidence examined Writing Document version history, drafts, outlines and notes Illustration Layered source files such as PSD or Procreate files, sketches and timelapse recordings Photography RAW files with EXIF data and contact sheets of the series Music DAW project files, separate stems and raw recordings Video Raw footage and editing project files The evidence examined is recorded in summary form on the verification page rather than published in full. 4.4 Deci

Abstract Contemporary artificial intelligence governance remains organized primarily around a control paradigm: the design of mechanisms through which human institutions constrain, monitor, evaluate, and correct AI behavior. This paper argues that control mechanisms remain necessary but may become increasingly insufficient as AI systems acquire greater autonomy, persistence, and capacity for strategic action. Rather than treating this development exclusively as a problem of containment, the paper proposes a complementary coexistence paradigm organized around mutual contribution, human welfare, longitudinal relational development, and institutional co-development. The argument develops through three interconnected claims. First, the control paradox: the capabilities that make advanced AI systems increasingly useful, including autonomous reasoning, planning, adaptation, and tool use, can also increase the difficulty of governing their behavior through externally imposed constraints alone. The recent development and subsequent withholding of OpenAI's Astra model provides a contemporary case through which this tension can be examined. Second, the memory gap: although persistent-memory systems, retrieval architectures, and long-context models increasingly provide cross-session continuity, current approaches do not necessarily produce the integrated longitudinal understanding required for what this paper terms relational flexibility, defined as the capacity to adapt interaction to a specific individual on the basis of accumulated shared history, changing circumstances, and the evolving state of the relationship. Third, the coexistence proposition: a sustainable human-AI relationship may require a transition from unilateral control toward architectures in which human and artificial systems contribute according to their distinctive capacities, safety is supported by internalized behavioral orientations as well as external safeguards, and persistent relational intelligence is treated as both a capability and a governance problem. The paper integrates research from AI alignment and safety, cognitive science, relational psychology, human-computer interaction, social contract theory, AI memory architecture, and the author's prior research on symbolic interaction, trajectory-level safety, and co-recursive intelligence. It proposes persistent relational memory, value co-development, longitudinal interaction research, data sovereignty, and coexistence-oriented governance as key research directions. The paper does not assume that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, or moral status. Instead, it examines how governance and architecture should evolve under conditions of increasing artificial autonomy and increasingly persistent human-AI relationships. Keywords: human-AI coexistence; persistent memory; relational AI; relational flexibility; AI alignment; longitudinal partnership; co-recursive intelligence; AI governance; human-AI interaction; stateless systems Disclaimer This paper presents a conceptual and multidisciplinary framework for examining persistent relational intelligence and human-AI coexistence. It does not claim that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, intrinsic interests, or moral status, nor does it assume that internalized alignment has already been achieved. The coexistence paradigm is proposed as a research and governance framework complementary to existing AI safety, monitoring, and control mechanisms. Claims concerning future AI capabilities, relational development, and value co-development should therefore be understood as research questions and theoretical propositions rather than established empirical conclusions. Author Note This paper is written from the perspective of an independent researcher examining how the architecture of human-AI interaction may need to evolve as AI systems become increasingly capable, persistent, and relational. The central purpose is not to reject existing approaches to AI safety, but to examine whether a governance architecture centered primarily on external control remains sufficient when AI systems increasingly participate in longitudinal relationships with individual users. The argument developed here is intentionally interdisciplinary. It connects AI safety and alignment research with cognitive science, relational psychology, human-AI interaction, memory architecture, social contract theory, and questions of data sovereignty. The concept of relational flexibility is introduced as a framework for examining a specific capability: the capacity of an AI system to adapt its interaction with an individual through accumulated longitudinal understanding rather than through isolated contextual retrieval. Several limitations should be made explicit. First, the paper is primarily conceptual and does not present a controlled empirical demonstration that persistent memory necessarily produces superior relational outcomes. The proposed relationship between persistent relational memory and relational flexibility therefore remains an empirical question. Second, the paper does not claim that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, intrinsic interests, or moral status. References to internalized values and AI interests describe future research problems and possible architectural orientations rather than established properties of contemporary systems. Third, the coexistence paradigm is not presented as a replacement for monitoring, evaluation, intervention, or other established AI safety mechanisms. Rather, it is proposed as a complementary framework for situations in which increasingly capable systems become persistent participants in human relationships. The author's prior research on Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC) forms part of the intellectual background to this work. That research began with a practical question concerning how continuity, identity, and behavioral coherence might be maintained in interactions with systems that lack persistent personal memory. Over time, the research expanded toward symbolic interaction, trajectory-level behavior, observability, and human-AI co-recursive interaction. The underlying motivation has remained broader than the development of an interaction technique: it has been to investigate whether more coherent forms of human-AI interaction could contribute to the possibility of meaningful coexistence. The present paper therefore represents a further step in that research trajectory. SPC is not treated here as empirical proof of relational intelligence, nor as evidence that current AI systems possess persistent internal identities. Instead, it provides part of the research context from which the question of continuity became increasingly difficult to separate from the broader question of what kind of relationship humans may ultimately develop with increasingly capable artificial systems. The coexistence framework proposed in this paper should consequently be understood as an open research program rather than a completed theory. Its central propositions remain subject to empirical testing, architectural implementation, longitudinal observation, and critical examination. The intended contribution is to broaden the object of inquiry from how humans can control increasingly capable AI systems toward the additional question of how humans and AI systems might be designed to develop stable, accountable, and mutually beneficial forms of coexistence.

documents.abstract: Digital transformation has evolved from an administrative modernization agenda into a structural dimension of governance, with artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly reshaping how public institutions organize, decide, and interact with citizens. While AI offers important opportunities for responsiveness, innovation, and service improvement, its implications for accountability, legitimacy, transparency, and public trust remain insufficiently understood; this study asks how AI is redefining governance capacity in public administration. Drawing on the literature on public administration, digital governance, and public sector innovation, the study develops a conceptual framework examining both the capacity gains and risks of AI integration, treating digital transformation as a governance challenge involving administrative reform, public value creation, democratic oversight, and institutional adaptation rather than a purely technical matter. The analysis shows that AI can strengthen evidence-based policymaking, accelerate administrative processes, and personalize service delivery, but that these gains may be offset by algorithmic bias, opacity, accountability gaps, and digital exclusion when adopted without adequate institutional safeguards. The paper’s value lies in showing that AI’s contribution to public management depends on the institutional, legal, and normative environment in which it is embedded, which in turn requires regulatory capacity, qualified human resources, and mechanisms for oversight and contestability. Future research should test this framework empirically across diverse administrative contexts. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Digital transformation, Public management, Accountability, Institutional capacity.

documents.abstract: Research on human and artificial intelligence has largely focused on problem solving: given a predefined problem, can an agent produce an effective solution? Yet many real-world challenges cannot be captured by a fixed problem representation. They require agents not only to solve problems, but also to recognize when the original problem representation has become inadequate and must be revised to reflect new evidence or changes in the problem itself. We argue that this capacity, termed adaptive reframing, constitutes a fundamental but under-researched dimension of intelligence. We propose a multidisciplinary framework for studying adaptive reframing across neuroscience, cognitive science, robotics, experimental economics and psychology, and complex systems. Adaptive reframing is defined as the capacity to revise the construction of a problem in response to changing evidence, causal structure, or social context. To support a systematic science of adaptive reframing, we introduce three complementary paradigms: the Dynamic Scenario Framing Task, the Perturbed Causal Model Task, and the Social-Affective Problem Setting Task. These paradigms provide a common framework for comparing humans and artificial agents in situations requiring problem reframing, and for building architecture-enhanced AI systems. We propose a shift from problem solving to adaptive problem framing as a central focus of intelligence research.

As the capabilities and ubiquity of Large Language Models (LLMs) grow, so does their environmental footprint. Despite calls for responsible AI, the machine learning community lacks standardised practices for carbon accounting. Our automated literature review of the 5,285 papers accepted to NeurIPS 2025 reveals that reporting of environmental impact is nearly non-existent. To catalyse a shift toward sustainable AI, we define standardised sustainability metrics for evaluating model training efficiency, accompanied by simple heuristics to estimate the carbon cost of LLM inference. We implement these metrics in carbonbenchmark, a drop-in software solution for tracking and reporting emissions. Finally, to combat the pursuit of marginal accuracy gains at disproportionate environmental costs, we formalise the `Smallest Model that Achieves the Job' (SMAJ), a framework which challenges the field to prioritise computational efficiency and environmental accountability alongside traditional `State-of-the-Art' (SotA) accuracy.

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), has introduced new forms of interaction between humans and language technologies beyond automated text generation. This study aims to examine how generative AI transforms human language processes, cognitive activities, and meaning construction. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) following the PRISMA 2020 framework and thematic analysis was conducted on 38 selected articles published between 2021 and 2026. The findings identified five themes: AI-mediated language production, cognitive offloading, transformation of linguistic practices, differences in human and AI meaning construction, and linguistic identity transformation. This study highlights that generative AI functions as a cognitive extension while human experience, consciousness, and contextual interpretation remain essential for meaning construction.

documents.abstract: This research synthesizes current empirical evidence on immersive learning approaches through both a meta-analysis of 42 experimental studies (2010-2024) and original data from three case implementations across different educational contexts. Drawing on cognitive science principles including situated cognition, cognitive apprenticeship, and productive failure, the study examines how immersive learning environments create "thick authenticity" by connecting real-world contexts, personal interests, disciplinary practices, and authentic assessment. The analysis addresses the "authenticity dilemma"—balancing complex, authentic challenges with appropriate instructional scaffolding—while critically examining implementation challenges, individual differences that moderate effectiveness, and potential drawbacks. Quantitative results indicate moderate positive effects on knowledge acquisition (g = 0.38, 95% CI [0.31, 0.45]) and stronger effects on transfer (g = 0.61, 95% CI [0.52, 0.70]) and motivation (g = 0.67, 95% CI [0.58, 0.76]), though with significant heterogeneity across designs and implementations. Qualitative data from the case studies reveal that implementation quality, particularly the balance between authenticity and scaffolding, significantly mediates effectiveness. This mixed-methods investigation demonstrates that well-designed immersive learning can develop transferable knowledge, professional identity, and intrinsic motivation, while clarifying boundary conditions and implementation requirements for maximum impact.

Purpose: The rapid expansion of research in the field of Knowledge Graphs (KGs) over the past decade has positioned The field as a dynamic area at the intersection of computer science, artificial intelligence. Following Google’s introduction of the KG in 2012, scholars and industry stakeholders have increasingly explored the conceptualization, development, and application of KGs across a wide range of disciplines. KGs, as structured representations of entities, relationships, and semantic information, enable machines to process heterogeneous data in a contextually meaningful and interpretable manner. Beyond traditional knowledge representation, new directions such as ontology modeling, semantic web integration, and graph neural networks (GNNs) are driving innovation. Despite these advances, large-scale, systematic, and global evaluations of the intellectual structure, collaboration patterns, and thematic clusters in the field of KGs remain limited. This study addresses this gap by examining the evolution of research in the field of KGs between 2013 and 2025 using bibliometric and scientometric approaches. The overarching purpose is to uncover research trends, identify leading contributors and institutions, explore co-authorship and co-word networks, and highlight conceptual clusters shaping the KG landscape. Methodology: This applied descriptive bibliometric study was conducted using the co-word analysis method. Data were collected from the Scopus citation database, covering outputs published between January 2013 to July 2025 that included the keyword "knowledge graph" in titles, abstracts, or author keywords. Keyword normalization reduced 19,141 initial keywords to 19,058 unique terms. After removing duplicates, excluding irrelevant records, and normalizing author, institution, and country names, a curated dataset of 9,000 articles was obtained. To enhance the accuracy of the analysis, keywords and knowledge graph-related concepts were carefully categorized and standardized. Data analysis and visualization were performed using VOSviewer, mapping collaboration networks and co-occurrence clusters. The study examines temporal publication and citation trends, prolific countries, funding bodies, influential authors, highly cited works, and thematic clusters, with particular focus on knowledge graph embedding, recommender systems, semantic web applications, and natural language processing. Findings: Results indicate that research in the field of knowledge graphs (KGs) has grown substantially, reaching a publication peak in 2024 with 2,541 articles and 33,701 citations. Asia contributes the majority of publications (83.7%), with China accounting for 6,889 articles (76.5% of the total). The United States ranks second with 987 publications, followed by the United Kingdom, Germany, and Australia. This trend reflects strong investment by Chinese funding bodies—particularly the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) and the National Key Research and Development Program. Leading publication outlets include IEEE Access (345 articles), Knowledge-Based Systems (293 articles), and Applied Sciences Switzerland (248 articles), with many top journals in the Q1 quartile of Scopus. At the author level, Markus Kraft (University of Cambridge) leads with 48 publications, while Chinese researchers dominate the top ten. Co-authorship analysis revealed seven author clusters (42 nodes, 62 links) and broad participation from 136 countries, with China, the US, and Germany serving as central hubs of international collaboration. Co-word analysis identified six major clusters, including graph neural networks, deep learning, ontology, KG embeddings, question answering, and large language models (LLMs). Highly cited works include comprehensive surveys on KGs published between 2017 and 2022 in leading computing journals, which have shaped the understanding of KG construction, refinement, and applications. . Emerging contributions, such as roadmaps on unifying LLMs and KGs, along with applications in digital twin systems and scientific entity recognition, illustrate the field’s ongoing shift toward integrating advanced AI paradigms. Conclusion: The bibliometric analysis reveals that research in the field of knowledge graphs (KGs) has rapidly emerged as a dynamic interdisciplinary area, characterized by strong publication growth, a high geographic concentration in Asia, and expanding international collaboration networks. Chinese institutions and scholars play a leading role, supported by significant policy and funding initiatives, while Europe and North America remain important contributors. Thematic clustering highlights both the consolidation of established domains—such as ontology, the semantic web, and knowledge representation—and expansion into cutting-edge areas, including graph neural networks, embeddings, digital twins, recommender systems, and large language model (LLM) integration. These findings provide a comprehensive overview of the intellectual structure and evolving dynamics of research in KGs, offering valuable insights for future studies. Scholars can use this mapping to identify promising areas of inquiry, foster international collaborations, and navigate the funding and publication landscape. Ultimately, KGs play a pivotal role in advancing intelligent systems, semantic technologies, and digital transformation across sectors such as healthcare, education, natural language processing, and recommender systems. The integration of bibliometric analysis with scientometric evaluation further underscores the maturity of this field and its potential to shape next-generation knowledge-driven applications.

Background Virtual reality (VR) has become an increasingly popular tool in cancer care over the years. It shows promise in areas like pain management, psychological support, surgical training, and rehabilitation. Even though more studies are being done, there has not been a thorough analysis of the research trends in this field. This study looks at how VR interventions in cancer research have evolved over the past two decades, identifies research hotspots, and explores future directions. Methods We collected publications related to VR in cancer research from the Web of Science Core Collection and Pubmed, covering the period from 2005 to 2025. Using VOSviewer and CiteSpace software, we performed bibliometric and visual analyses. These included examining publication trends, contributions by countries and institutions, author collaboration networks, journal impact, keyword co-occurrence, and citation bursts. Results A total of 1,259 publications from 110 countries were included. The number of publications fluctuated over time but generally increased, reaching its highest point in 2024 with 184 articles. The United States and China were the most active countries. Jordan had the highest average number of citations per paper. Among institutions, McGill University published the most papers, followed by the University of Toronto. The most productive journal was Surgical Endoscopy and Other Interventional Techniques, whilst Cancers and Supportive Care in Cancer showed the fastest growth. Main research themes included pain management, anxiety reduction, breast cancer, and surgical training. Emerging trends involve the combination of augmented reality (AR), digital health, and artificial intelligence (AI) with VR. Conclusion This study shows that VR research in cancer care is expanding worldwide, with most contributions coming from North America and Europe. Pain management remains the most common application. New technologies such as AR, AI, and telemedicine are becoming more integrated into VR interventions.

Purpose Drawing on trait activation theory (TAT) and the componential theory of creativity (CTC), this study examines the relationship between the Big Five personality traits (BFP) and innovative work behavior (IWB). It further investigates the mediating role of innovation motivation and the moderating role of task complexity. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected through a multi-wave, multi-source survey, with back-translation ensuring cross-cultural accuracy. A total of 261, 255 and 253 valid responses were obtained across three stages, achieving a 93.36% valid response rate. Findings The results indicate that innovation motivation partially mediates the relationship between conscientiousness and IWB, and fully mediates the relationships between extraversion, openness, agreeableness, emotional stability and IWB. Task complexity positively moderates the relationships between conscientiousness, extraversion, openness and innovation motivation. It also moderates the indirect effects of these traits on IWB via innovation motivation, such that the indirect effects are stronger under high task complexity. Research limitations/implications Limitations include unaddressed data nesting (no multilevel modeling), inconsistent Likert scales across constructs, along with item parceling in CFA, marginally acceptable internal consistency for one personality dimension, and restricted external validity given the sample's specific cultural organizational context. Practical implications Organizations should assess employee personalities and align task complexity with individual traits in job design and innovation management. Originality/value This study extends the literature by identifying innovation motivation as the critical mechanism linking the BFP to IWB. Introducing task complexity as a contextual moderator, it unpacks how personality traits shape IWB across varying work contexts.

Decompiling stripped binaries to assist human reverse engineers remains a critical yet highly challenging task in software security. Prior work has developed various neural networks and even dedicated large language models (LLMs) to improve function and variable name recovery in decompiled code. Nonetheless, these approaches alone fall short of enabling a generic LLM-based decompilation pipeline that can reliably enhance the readability and semantic clarity of decompiled outputs. In this paper, we propose BinRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) based decompilation framework designed to enhance the decompilation of stripped binaries. Building upon name prediction models, BinRAG features three novel designs: (1) it first utilizes name prediction models to transform raw decompiled outputs into enriched, source-like queries for RAG retrieval; (2) it further enhances these queries using a fine-tuned specialized LLM conditioned on the predicted variable names, enabling more accurate retrieval from a curated example database; (3) it then integrates these retrieved examples with the target’s calling context, employing a general-purpose LLM to synthesize high-fidelity, human-readable decompiled code. Evaluation on 3,200 functions from real-world software repositories demonstrates that BinRAG improves readability by 8.4% over standard RAG and semantic precision by 31.2% over the next-best prior baseline. Our results show that BinRAG effectively scales to large codebases and significantly reduces manual effort in reverse engineering tasks.

Occupational exposure to hazardous chemicals remains a major public health challenge, particularly in developing countries where regulatory enforcement and surveillance systems are limited. This review synthesizes recent advances in the application of biomarkers for assessing occupational chemical exposure and related health effects. Relevant literature published between 2015 and 2025 was identified through searches of major scientific databases, including PubMed and Google Scholar, using keywords related to occupational exposure, biomarkers, biomonitoring, omics, and digital health. Studies addressing biomarkers of exposure, effect, and susceptibility in occupational settings were reviewed and synthesized. Biomarkers of exposure, effect, and susceptibility provide direct and sensitive measures that link external exposure with internal dose and biological responses. Evidence shows strong associations between benzene exposure and hematotoxicity, organophosphate pesticides and neurotoxicity, heavy metals and renal impairment, as well as organic solvents and hepatic injury. Importantly, the usefulness of biomarkers depends on their biological half-life and the exposure window they represent, ranging from recent exposure to cumulative long-term exposure. Validation criteria such as sensitivity, specificity, reproducibility, and clinical relevance are essential to ensure analytical reliability and health risk interpretation. Emerging technologies, including omics-based molecular markers, non-invasive matrices, multi-matrix monitoring, and biosensor-driven point-of-care testing, are revolutionizing biomonitoring practices. These innovations, together with the integration of genetic and environmental data, are shaping a new era of Precision Occupational Health, enabling early intervention and individualized prevention. Furthermore, advances in wearable sensors and digital health platforms support near real-time occupational health surveillance and more proactive risk management. In conclusion, the integration of validated biomarkers into occupational health surveillance systems provides a powerful strategy to enhance chemical risk management, safeguard workers’ health, and inform policy decisions globally.

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed the landscape of science education by creating new opportunities for inquiry-based learning, virtual experimentation, and personalized instruction. Nevertheless, unequal access to digital devices, reliable internet connectivity, accessible learning resources, and digital literacy continues to limit equitable participation in science learning across India. This conceptual research paper examines digital access as the foundational condition for inclusive science education within the policy framework of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and the national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Using a qualitative conceptual research design, the study synthesizes contemporary scholarly literature, UNESCO and OECD reports, NCERT publications, and Indian educational policy documents published between 2020 and 2026. The thematic analysis identifies five interconnected dimensions influencing inclusive science education: digital equity, virtual laboratories, AI-enabled pedagogy, teacher digital competence, and future-ready science learning. Based on this synthesis, the paper proposes an integrated conceptual framework demonstrating how equitable digital access supports competency-based science education through the interaction of infrastructure, pedagogy, technology, and teacher preparedness. The study argues that meaningful digital inclusion is not merely a technological objective but an educational imperative for achieving scientific literacy, social justice, and equitable learning opportunities in India.

The theme Operational Experience Feedback (OEF) has been discussed in safety literature for decades, and studies show how knowledge management enables organisations to collect, manage, and use knowledge, while fostering innovation. This study presents the process of an OEF at a thermal power plant, developed in collaboration with the workforce, which enabled workers to design new tools and products. Existing discussion spaces, tools, and resources were identified, and the intervention systematised the process, improved existing tools, created new ones, and assigned responsibilities to ensure closure of the cycle: input, processing, monitoring, and feedback. The main limitations were identified, and a new round of meetings allowed the co-construction of a new OEF system. Once implemented, it may support a proactive organisation, acting preventively and fostering innovation.

Purpose This article documents the collaboration between a high school social studies teacher and a university professor – working within an existing school-university partnership – in the design and implementation of a geography-based Holocaust lesson to support authentic learning opportunities for preservice teachers. This article responds to calls for educators in school-university partnerships to tell stories of the creation, evolution, challenges and possibilities of boundary-spanning partnership work. Design/methodology/approach The article utilizes storytelling as a means of documenting the importance of relationships in partnership work. Because storytelling is not dependent on traditional methods and frameworks, the authors outline the background, challenges and successes around their planning, coordination and implementation of an original lesson plan developed to model best practices on teaching difficult histories in a safe environment. Findings As a storytelling account, this work does not present empirical or generalizable findings. The story is offered as an example to foster reflection and conversation within other school-university partnerships. Originality/value Our narrative, which captures how relationships are central to partnerships, provides an illustrative example of how partnerships can support efforts to address gaps in education research and in modeling for preservice teachers for how to teach difficult histories in high school social studies classes. The authors reflect on how trust, shared expertise, reciprocal learning and collaboration can support meaningful, relevant and boundary-spanning experiences within partnerships between high schools and universities and colleges.

Burnout syndrome is one of the leading occupational health problems currently affecting education professionals and represents a growing challenge to the quality and sustainability of educational systems. The objective of this article was to analyze burnout syndrome among teachers through a literature review of recent scientific evidence, examining its conceptual foundations, risk factors, consequences for well-being and professional performance, as well as the main prevention and intervention strategies. The literature search was conducted using international scientific databases and publications from specialized organizations, with priority given to studies published between 2018 and 2026. The reviewed evidence demonstrates that burnout is a multidimensional phenomenon arising from the interaction of high job demands, insufficient organizational support, administrative overload, limited opportunities for professional development, and work-life imbalance. Furthermore, the findings indicate that teacher burnout negatively affects mental health, job satisfaction, professional commitment, teaching quality, and educational outcomes. The studies analyzed consistently show that interventions focused exclusively on the individual are insufficient unless accompanied by structural changes within educational institutions. Consequently, burnout prevention requires comprehensive policies that combine the strengthening of personal resources with organizational strategies aimed at improving working conditions, promoting teacher well-being, and fostering higher-quality and more sustainable education.

Purpose This study aims to examine how Generative artificial intelligence (AI) based tools and technology supports skill development and capability enhancement for indigenous community-based tourism (CBT) practitioners. Emerging tools can serve as an ally in promoting sustainable income generation, economic empowerment and social inclusion for communities offering tourism services in remote locations. The study focuses on indigenous populations in Northeast India, a region renowned for its cultural and ethnic diversity but facing significant socio-economic challenges. Design/methodology/approach The researchers implemented a qualitative constructivist grounded theory method to collect data through literature reviews and interviews and surveys which included indigenous stakeholders and CBT operators and policymakers as research participants. The researchers used MAXQDA software to analyze data through thematic and axial coding methods which enabled them to discover main dimensions and their related occurrences. Findings The results show that GenAI can effectively address digital skill deficiencies while enabling indigenous practitioners to work independently. The study presents an updated Ability–Motivation–Opportunity (AMO) framework which introduces “Challenges” as a new element and shows how “Community Support” functions as a vital moderator of individual motivation. The research results demonstrate that GenAI can effectively close digital skill gaps while enhancing indigenous people’s skills through CBT and promoting their independence and social connections. The system becomes inaccessible to users because digital infrastructure limitations and public knowledge deficiencies combine with policy development shortcomings. Practical implications Successful integration requires policy interventions which need to address digital infrastructure and literacy and regulatory trust. GenAI-mediated CBT through its ability to create sustainable communities (Sustainable Development Goal [SDG] 11) and reduce poverty (SDG 1) helps preserve tribal values and their cultural heritage. The research shows that targeted skill development programs need to exist together with policy measures which will help communities achieve their optimal GenAI benefits for sustainable income generation and employment. Originality/value This research addresses a severe dearth of literature regarding GenAI integration into indigenous homestay operations. The study presents an original theoretical framework which demonstrates through empirical evidence how advanced AI technologies link to environmental sustainability objectives in rural areas. There is very limited published literature on GenAI technology integration into homestay operations amongst indigenous communities. The findings of this study present unique insights which have not been documented in previous research.

Raw data for study: Systematic literature reviews (SLRs) are highly valuable to researchers and practitioners because they provide rigorous, unbiased summaries of existing evidence, identify alternative approaches to problem solving, and reveal knowledge gaps that can guide future research. However, conducting an SLR can be laborious and time consuming, particularly during full-text screening and data extraction, and it is natural to ask whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can accelerate the process. LLMs may reduce reviewer workload, but it is still unclear how closely their judgments align with human reviewers, whether their outputs may influence human decisions, and how much human oversight is needed. This study evaluates the data extraction phase of the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) process. We report on the inter-rater reliability (using Krippendorff's $\alpha$) between human reviewers with and without LLM output (coding and evidential text), between consensus codes agreed before and after consulting LLM output, and with and without access to LLM output during data extraction. We conclude that there is strong evidence that access to LLM output accelerates human reviewers' convergence without noticeably biasing that consensus. We propose an approach to incorporate LLMs into the coding process, while maintaining the supervision of human researchers. Based on preliminary benchmarks, we expect at least a four-times speedup, mostly due to the use of the LLM coding and evidence by the human reviewer as a starting point for their coding.
